en: The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Dhāraṇī of the Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Extracted from the Vajrayoga Tantra;
by the Grand Master of the Court, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple, who was the Duke of Sū, with a fief of three thousand households, invested with purple robes, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bearing the title of Great Mirror (Dàjiàn), and the epithet of Great Universal Wisdom (Dàguǎngzhì). 1. Elucidating the Manifestation of the Majestic Power of the Five Bodhisattvas, Part One. Elucidating the Manifestation of the Majestic Power of the Five Bodhisattvas, Part One. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi of the East. *Vajrapāṇi-bodhisattva-mahāsattva-sūtra* of the East. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi of the East.
Holding a vajra in his hand, he emits blue light and departs with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that kingdom.
The commentary explains: "Vajrapāṇi" means...
According to the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra* in its original Sanskrit version held by the Tripitaka masters, it is said:
"Firmness and utility possess two meanings.
Relying on that sūtra:
However, the manifestations of these five bodhisattvas differ according to two kinds of wheels.
The first is the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*),
which manifests the body of reality (*tathatā-kāya*).
Because the body is obtained as the fruition of the vows practiced, there is second,
the wheel of instruction and command,
which manifests a wrathful body.
Because he manifests fierce power out of great compassion,
this Vajrapāṇi is none other than the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
He holds a vajra in his hand.
The manifestation of correct wisdom is like a vajra,
for it is able to sever the subtle obstructions of self and phenomena; thus,
it is manifested through the turning of the wheel of the teachings.
The wrathful Trailokyavijaya Vajra has four heads and eight arms;
he subdues all the demonic hosts of Maheśvara, the Great Lord Śiva.
It is for the purpose of subduing those who violate the True Dharma and harm sentient beings.
As for the emission of blue light,
it manifests the ability to dispel hosts such as Māras.
Together with the Eastern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his retinue of immeasurable gandharvas and piśācas,
he went with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land.
Second, in the south, is the Bodhisattva Vajraratna; the Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Vajraratna in the South: [it concerns] the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajraratna in the South.
Holding a vajra-maṇi that emits light with the color of the sun, he went with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land.
The commentary explains: as for the term "vajra-jewel," it refers to...
As that sutra states regarding the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:
relying on the aforementioned wheel of Dharma, he manifests a supreme and wondrous body,
cultivating practices such as giving with the three wheels purified.
"Holder of the vajra-maṇi. In Sanskrit, *maṇi* is translated as "jewel" (*bǎo*).
Its substance is pure, firm, and dense, just like a vajra.
This is the Vajra-Cintāmaṇi; whatever sentient beings seek, they shall obtain it all.
In accordance with the wheel of command, he manifests as the wrathful Vajra-Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
He manifests eight arms in order to subdue all the hosts of asuras, retinues,
and malevolent spirits who afflict sentient beings by spreading pestilence, thereby bringing them under control.
The emission of solar light signifies his ability to dispel the asuras and other such beings.
He has the Southern King Virūḍhaka and an immeasurable host of kumbhāṇḍas and pretas as his retinue.
Regarding "four koṭis":
first, as for one *koṭi*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that one hundred *lakṣas* constitute one *koṭi*;
this corresponds to the number of ten billion (*bǎiyì*) in this region.
The remaining three koṭis should all be understood accordingly.
Together with such a multitude, they went to protect that kingdom.
Third, from the west, the Bodhisattva Vajratīkṣṇa; third, from the west, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajratīkṣṇa. According to the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajratīkṣṇa* from the west.
Holding a vajra-sword, he emits golden light and,
together with four koṭis of bodhisattvas, goes to protect that land.
The commentary explains that "vajra-sharp" means:
As that sūtra states regarding the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"By means of the aforementioned wheel of Dharma, he manifests a supreme and wondrous body;
for his perfect wisdom is complete and he has attained mastery."
The one who holds the vajra-sword demonstrates that his activity is able to sever the innate obscurations of both self and others; thus,
by means of the wheel of command, he manifests as the wrathful six-legged Vajra.
Each arm has six [hands], and they sit upon water buffaloes;
this is for the purpose of subduing all evil and venomous nāgas and taming those who raise fierce winds and rains to harm sentient beings.
The emission of golden light signifies his ability to dispel malevolent nāgas and the like.
He has as his retinue the Western Guardian King Virūpākṣa and an immeasurable multitude of nāgas and piśācas.
He went with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land.
Fourth, the Bodhisattva Vajrayakṣa of the North; according to the *Vajrayakṣa-bodhisattva-mahāsattva-sūtra*, [he is] the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrayakṣa of the North.
Holding a vajra bell, he emits light of lapis lazuli color and departs with four koṭis of yakṣas to protect that kingdom.
The commentary explains: the Sanskrit term *yakṣa* is translated here as "majestic power" (*weide*).
Furthermore, it is translated as "exhaustion," because it can exhaust all enmities.
As that sutra says: "The Bodhisattva who subdues all Māras and enemies."
Relying on the aforementioned wheel of Dharma, he manifests a supreme and wondrous body;
because his knowledge of activities is perfected and he has attained mastery,
he holds a vajra bell in his hand.
Its sound resounds to awaken sentient beings,
manifesting through Prajñā to alert the deluded multitudes; thus,
by means of the wheel of the teaching-command, it appears as the Wrathful Purifying Body Vajra.
He manifests four arms to subdue all terrifying yakṣas,
constantly seeking opportunities by day and night.
The emission of light in the color of lapis lazuli signifies the ability to subdue those who rob others of their vital energy and harm sentient beings,
and to dispel yakṣas and other such spirits.
Together with Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, and his retinue of immeasurable yakṣas and rākṣasas,
he went with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land.
The fifth, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāramitā, from the *Vajrapāramitā Sūtra* within the Central Section.
Holding a vajra-wheel in his hand, he emits five-colored light and departs with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that kingdom.
The commentary explains: as for the term "Vajrapāramitā," it refers to this.
This refers to "reaching the other shore.
As that sutra says, it is the Bodhisattva Turning the Dharma Wheel.
Based on the aforementioned Dharma wheel, he manifests a supreme and wondrous body.
With his practices and vows fulfilled, he abides in the state of perfect enlightenment.
As for the one holding a vajra-wheel in his hand:
this refers to Vairocana when he first attained perfect awakening.
It is requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned for the sake of manifestation;
furthermore, it is so that sentient beings may be transformed and guided by the Wheel of Dharma,
leading countless and immeasurable beings to the further shore.
In accordance with the wheel of command, he manifests as the wrathful Akṣobhyavajra to subdue all malevolent spirits, delusions,
and those who cause obstacles and affliction, thereby bringing them under control.
The emission of five-colored light manifests the possession of manifold virtues and the destruction of the aforementioned darknesses.
He is accompanied by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and an immeasurable host of devas as his retinue.
He went together with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land. Chapter Two:

Establishing the Ritual Procedures for the Maṇḍala. Now, by relying on this sūtra to establish the maṇḍala, one protects the nation, the family, and the individual, eliminates calamities, and transforms obstacles; thus, from the state of an ordinary being, one attains sainthood.
For one who practices yoga to reach the ultimate maṇḍala,
it is most excellent to first choose a place that is peaceful, clean, and where śarīras are present.
Whether in a secluded chamber, or in a mountain forest or rock cave;
or at a place where two rivers converge;
or by a garden grove abounding in flowers and fruit, or beside a lotus pond.
Or at a place where sages and saints attained the Way,
or at a place beloved by practitioners,
or upon a boat, or atop a multi-storied pavilion, or upon a flat rock.
Or beneath trees in a pleasing grove—
in such places as these— one should establish the maṇḍala on an auspicious day.
Dig the ground to a depth of two cubits, with a width of four, six, or even twelve cubits.
Remove all tiles, rubble, hair, fur, ash, bones, and all other miscellaneous impurities; they must be cleared away entirely.
Separately take soil from the two banks of a pure river,
and construct a mandala according to the ritual rules;
ensure that the excavated site is free from all impure substances.
Then fill it with the original earth.
If there is any surplus soil, it is the most excellent ground;
pray that [your] vows may be swiftly fulfilled.
If the filling is level and full, that ground is of medium quality;
thus, one's wishes will be middling.
If the filling is insufficient, that ground is inferior.
One's aspirations will be delayed and difficult to fulfill;
[the ground] must be filled and leveled until it is perfectly smooth.
Just as with the base of a śarīra stūpa, on a boat, atop a multi-storied pavilion, upon a flat rock, or on ground that is secluded, pure, and free from impurities,
one should simply establish the maṇḍala according to the dharma.
Then there is no need to dig.
Once the center of the mandala has been leveled and filled, select an auspicious day during the first watch of the day and dig a pit one foot deep,
with the same dimensions in length and breadth.
Place small portions of the seeds of the five grains and various fragrant medicinal herbs therein,
and recite the Earth Deity mantra as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ picchiviyai svāhā.* Recite this twenty-one times to consecrate the incense and other offerings.
Place [the materials] therein and fill it with earth until level.
Next, sit upon the altar facing east.
At the center of the altar, measure one cubit in both length and breadth.
Take various fragrant waters and smear them upon a circular mandala;
scatter seasonal flowers all over its surface,
as well as milk porridge, precious fruits, and various foods and drinks.
With a sincere heart, make offerings and press your right hand upon the altar.
Recite the mantra of the Earth Deity one hundred and eight times, and then speak this verse:
"O Deva, you who have personally realized the state of Perfect Enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha, I now establish this maṇḍala; may you grant your constant protection.
Recite this verse three times.
Then, taking cow dung that has not fallen to the ground,
mix it with pure substances and various fragrant waters;
recite the aforementioned mantra twenty-one times to empower it.
Then, starting from the northeast corner of the altar,
he should gradually apply [the ointment] with his right hand, circling clockwise according to the ritual rules.
He must recite the aforementioned mantra continuously until the application of the altar is completed, without interruption.
Do not speak otherwise.
Once the mandala has dried,
again follow the previous method, using exclusively the juice of *gomaya* (cow dung).
Apply a second layer as before;
recite the aforementioned mantra in its entirety as previously described.
Once it has dried:
Furthermore, take the leaves of the lotus-seed plant, or the hibiscus, or the *sūryavallī* (nightshade),
and pound them to rub and adorn the altar,
first purifying it. Next, spread a blue canopy over the altar.
Measure the dimensions of the maṇḍala.
Hang twenty-four banners around the maṇḍala.
Next, within the maṇḍala, have the artist bathe, put on fresh clean clothes, and receive the upavāsa precepts according to the dharma before performing the colored paintings.
The altar has three tiers.
Do not use leather glue; use various fragrant glues. If fragrant glue is unavailable, [use other suitable adhesives].
Boil glutinous rice water and use it to mix with the colors.
In the center of the mandala, draw a wheel with twelve spokes;
in the east, draw a five-pronged vajra.
On the southern side, paint the Vajraratna;
on the western side, paint the Vajrakhadga;
and on the northern side, paint the Vajraghaṇṭā.
These five aforementioned matters are the secret mudrās held in the hands of the Bodhisattvas of the five directions.
In the southeast corner, draw a three-pronged vajra;
in the southwest corner, draw a jeweled crown.
In the northwest corner, draw a *vīṇā* lute;
in the northeast corner, draw a *karmavajra*.
At each of the four corners, place four auspicious jars (*bhadraghaṭa*).
Gold, silver, copper, porcelain, or even new earthenware may be used;
it should hold no more than one *sheng*.
Fill the vessel with water and insert flowering branches.
Use four types of silk cloth, each four chi in length—
blue, yellow, red, and green— and tie them to the necks of the four vases in that order.
Next, at the third level, draw a vajra-hook on the eastern gate.
On the southern gate, paint the Vajrapāśa;
on the western gate, paint the Vajrasphoṭa;
on the northern gate, paint the Vajraghaṇṭā.
In the southeast corner, paint an incense burner;
in the southwest corner, paint lotus leaves;
and in the center, paint various flowers.
In the northwest corner, draw a lamp;
in the northeast corner, draw an incense-ointment vessel.
All the vajras and other items drawn therein are adorned with flames.
Outside the threefold altar is a single-layered boundary path;
on its four sides, draw gates aligned with the outer boundary path.
Drive stakes of khadira wood into the four corners of the maṇḍala;
if such wood is unavailable, iron or stakes of red sandalwood may also be used.
They should be twelve finger-widths long and driven four finger-widths into the ground.
Recite the third Vajra mantra below twenty-one times to consecrate the stakes,
and then drive them in.
Have a young girl join five-colored threads together,
with a thickness like that of a small finger,
and bind them around the head of the stake upon the perimeter of the altar.
Place four incense burners at the four gates of the *stūpa* and burn incenses such as agallochum,
sandalwood, frankincense, and ghee-blended incense.
At the four corners of the *stūpa*, draw three-pronged half-vajras.
On each of the four corners, light one lamp. Outside the four gates, on both the left and right sides,
place two porcelain bowls— gold, silver, or copper are all acceptable— to hold *argha* water with fragrant incense.
Change the water at every session.
Sprinkle it in a clean place and do not tread upon it.
If one wishes to perform the rite for seven days, fourteen days, or even up to forty-nine days:
Thus, every morning, he reverently made offerings of eight bowls of milk porridge, eight bowls of curd-rice, eight layers of precious fruits,
and eight layers of sweet, crisp delicacies— fresh and pure each day.
If one does not require formal prayers,
one may perform ordinary offerings by burning incense, lighting lamps, offering *argha* water, and applying fragrant unguents,
as well as daily offerings of freshly gathered flowers.
On the fourteenth and fifteenth days of each month,
on these two days, one should perform offerings as described above with congee, rice, fruits, and so forth.
For those who wish to eliminate calamities for the sake of the nation, the family,
or themselves, they should sit facing north and visualize the deity and all offerings as being white in color.
Recite silently in a state of tranquility.
To seek increase (puṣṭi), sit facing east and visualize the principal deity and all others as being yellow in color.
With a joyful and tranquil mind, one recites silently without making a sound.
To subdue [an opponent], one sits facing south and visualizes the deity and others as being blue-black in color.
Arousing great compassion within while manifesting fierce wrath without,
one should recite with a loud voice,
facing west, in order to seek reverence and affection.
Visualize the principal deity and others as being entirely red in color.
Recite the mantra aloud with a mind of joy and anger.
According to these four types [of practice], if it is for the rite of pacification (śāntika):
From the first day of the month to the eighth day,
if one seeks increase;
from the ninth day of the month to the fifteenth day.
If one seeks to win over others through affection,
[one should practice] from the sixteenth to the twenty-second day; if for the purpose of subjugation, [one should practice during the remaining days].
From the twenty-third day until the end of the month,
the establishment of the *maṇḍala* concludes and begins again;
however, if there is an urgent necessity, one must not rely on these fixed dates.
However, the divisions of day and night are established according to the time:
for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one takes the first part of the night;
for rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one takes the first part of the day.
If for the purpose of attraction and love, one should take the latter part of the night;
if for subjugation, one should take midday or midnight.
These four types apply to the construction of a maṇḍala, as well as recitation, prayer, and so forth.
Based on the aforementioned times and dates as a regular practice, those who seek liberation and supreme enlightenment and cultivate yoga should do so during four periods of the day and night:
the late night, midday, dusk, and midnight.
Offering with a devoted mind is the most supreme and excellent.
[The reason for] drawing the mandala below [this section] is because people might otherwise find it difficult to understand.
3. The Ritual Procedures for Entering the Maṇḍala. Third: The Ritual Procedures for Entering the Maṇḍala. If a practitioner seeks to pacify calamities (śāntika),...
First, one must bathe and put on new, clean clothes.
If one is a layperson receiving the upavāsa precepts,
one should give rise to a profound mind of Mahāyāna.
If one seeks accomplishment, one should not begrudge even body or life.
One should give rise to a vast heart of compassionate vows to deliver infinite sentient beings.
Those who can act in this way will swiftly attain accomplishment.
Having entered the dharma hall, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and universally pay homage to all the Triple Gem throughout the entire dharma realm.
With the right knee touching the ground, repent for all karmic obstacles of the three types of action.
Exhorting the Buddhas of the ten directions to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma;
requesting all Tathāgatas to remain long in the world;
and rejoicing in the merit and wisdom cultivated by those of the three vehicles.
By means of all the merit I, [Name], have cultivated,
I dedicate it entirely toward unexcelled bodhi;
may it be shared with all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma realm.
The siddhis sought shall be swiftly fulfilled.
Next, assume the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
If circumstances prevent it, one need not perform a ritual bath.
With both hands smeared with fragrant unguents, generate a mind of earnest devotion and form the Seal of Purity (*viśuddhi-mudrā*).
Holding the two hands at the heart with palms joined hollowly like an unfurled lotus, recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ svabhāva-śuddhāḥ sarva-dharmāḥ svabhāva-śuddho ’haṃ. Recite this mantra three times.
While reciting, one should direct the mind to pervade extensively:
"All dharmas are originally pure; therefore, my own body is also entirely pure."
He then closed his eyes and focused his mind,
visualizing all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas within their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment throughout the entirety of space,
holding various kinds of supreme and exquisite incense and flowers.
With the utmost sincerity of the three karmas, prostrate with the head to pay homage.
First, bind the Samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family: for the first binding of the Buddha Family Samaya-mudrā, place both hands at the heart with the fingers interlaced inwardly to form fists.
Then, holding up both thumbs, recite the mantra:
Oṃ kṣaṇakṣaṇa svāhā. Recite this mantra three times, pronouncing it without sound.
The following cases are to be understood accordingly.
One scatters [the flowers] upon the crown of the head;
by binding this mudrā and reciting this Buddha-family samaya mantra, [the purpose is accomplished].
All Buddhas of the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm gather like clouds, filling the void,
and empower the practitioner to be free from all obstacles and afflictions.
Through the purity of the three karmas, may the practices and vows be swiftly accomplished.
Second, for binding the Samaya-mudrā of all Bodhisattva families: for the second binding of the Samaya-mudrā of all Bodhisattva families, place both hands at the heart as before and form fists.
Bend the left thumb into the palm and recite the mantra:
Oṃ āḥ luḥ ka svāhā. Recite this three times as before, then release the mudrā over the crown of the head.
By binding this mudrā and reciting these samaya mantras of the various bodhisattva families,
one immediately attains [the presence of] Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and all the bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm.
They all gathered like clouds, filling the entirety of space.
They empowered the practitioner so that their three karmas became pure and free from all calamities;
this was because the Bodhisattvas had undertaken their original vows of compassion.
Now, all that is sought shall be completely fulfilled.
Third, binding the Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Family: for the third binding of the Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Family, form the mudrā as before with the right hand, and extend the left thumb.
Bend the right thumb into the palm and recite the mantra:
Oṃ vajrādṛḍhaka svāhā. Recite this three times as before and scatter [the mudrā] over the crown of the head.
By forming the mudrā and reciting the Vajra Family Samaya mantra,
all the vajras of the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm immediately manifest in wrathful forms and assemble like clouds.
The entire realm of empty space empowers the practitioner,
making their three karmas as steadfast as a vajra;
that is to say, those noble ones receive the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
By the power of one's own vows, on a grand scale, it protects and sustains the national borders so that no calamities occur;
on a small scale, it ensures that even a single person is free from all misfortunes.
Fourth, the Sealing and Protecting the Body Mudrā: Furthermore, employ the mudrās bound by the three families.
Then, while reciting the mantra, perform consecration at five places—
namely, the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat—
and scatter [the offerings] upon the crown of the head.
One immediately becomes clad in the adamantine, firm armor.
Through this empowerment, the body of the Wandering One (Parivrājaka) blazes with majestic radiance,
such that all māras who create obstacles and afflictions [are overcome].
The eyes did not dare to look upon it, and they fled away quickly.

Fifth, the mudrā for expelling obstacles and the mudrā for the precious boundary of the vajra directions: for the fifth, the mudrā for expelling obstacles and the mudrā for the precious boundary of the vajra directions, use the aforementioned mudrās of the Vajra Family as before.
Reciting that mantra, one circumambulates the maṇḍala three times to the left;
this will immediately cause all powerful māras who follow the Buddha and Bodhisattvas and are capable of appearing or disappearing at will to depart for other realms.
Following the mind, one circumambulates three times to the right while voiding urine or excrement;
this immediately constitutes a vajra boundary of precious corners,
which even all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not transgress.
How much more so for those who create obstacles and afflictions, who can find no opportunity [to harm].
[The mudrā for scattering upon the crown of the head.
The sixth binding: the mudrā for inviting the assembly of sages to descend upon the altar. For the right hand, employ the three preceding mudrās and mantras of the three families.
Pointing the index finger toward oneself,
one summons three times and beckons three times;
immediately, the holy assemblies of the three families fill the space before one.
Each remains in its own position, dwelling in silence without obstructing one another.
[The mudrā for scattering upon the crown:
The seventh mudrā for offering scented *argha* water: with both hands, hold and support a *maṇi* jewel vessel on the right.
Fill a vessel with scented water and place it between the eyebrows; recite the mantra:
Oṃ vāruṇāya hūṃ. Recite this three times while extending the mind to pervade [the area].
In succession, bathe all the noble assembly universally,
scattering [the water] upon their crowns;
by means of this offering of argha, [may they be purified].
From the stage of practice through aspiration up to the stage of the cloud of dharma,
throughout each and every stage, one receives the protection of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions of the dharma-realm and attains all empowerments.
The eighth mudrā for offering the precious throne: With both hands at the heart, join the palms with hollowed fingers.
The two thumbs and the two little fingers are placed side by side and slightly bent.
The remaining six fingers are each slightly spread and bent, like a blossoming lotus flower. The mantra is:
Oṃ kamala svāhā. One should form this mudrā and recite the mantra.
By causing the assembly of noble beings to accept and enjoy the offered precious throne as it truly is,
the practitioner shall reach the state of fruition and obtain a vajra-solid precious throne.
Ninth, the mudrā of Universal Offering: Join the two hands in *añjali*;
interlace the five fingers with the right over the left.
Place it upon the heart and recite the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ svāhā oṃ udgata-sphara hīṃ gaganakhe svāhā*. By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, [the purpose is accomplished].
Extending his mind widely,
he pervaded the ocean-like assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the entire Dharma-realm,
raining down all manner of offerings everywhere.
Recite the first time:
imagine that countless sand-like precious vessels are filled with powdered incense, which universally coats the assembly of holy ones.
Recite the second time.
Adorned everywhere with various flower garlands,
recite for the third time,
burning various incenses as a universal offering.
Upon reciting for the fourth time,
various sublime foods and drinks from among the heavens will rain down;
these shall be placed in precious vessels and offered everywhere as an act of universal worship.
Recite for the fifth time.
Rain down various maṇi jewels as lamps and light,
making universal offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
By the power of the empowerment through reciting the mantra,
the incense and other offerings presented are all truly enjoyed by the assembly of noble ones in the ocean-like gathering.
The practitioner shall always obtain [this] in the future.
This is the tenth: the Root Mudrā of the Prajñāpāramitā. To form the tenth Root Mudrā of the Prajñāpāramitā, again place the backs of both hands together.
Draw back the two index fingers;
bend the two little fingers into the palms;
and press the tips of the two index fingers with the thumbs respectively.
Place it upon the heart and recite the dhāraṇī from within the sūtra seven times.
By forming this mudrā and reciting the dhāraṇī,
the practitioner’s own body immediately transforms into the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā.
She is the mother of all Buddhas.
Her Bodhisattva image sits in the full lotus posture upon a white lotus flower,
her body the color of golden-yellow.
Her body is adorned all over with various real jewel necklaces;
she wears a jeweled crown upon her head, from which white silk ribbons hang down on both sides.
Her left hand is held at her heart, grasping a Sanskrit manuscript of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Place the right hand at the breast in the *dharmacakra-mudrā*,
pressing the tip of the ring finger with the thumb.
Then, visualize the Bodhisattva from head to foot.
From all the pores of his body, rays of light flowed forth,
manifesting in various colors that filled the entire Dharma-realm.
Within each ray of light, he manifested immeasurable Buddhas who pervaded the realm of empty space.
Throughout all world-systems, for the sake of sentient beings everywhere,
they shall proclaim the profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā according to their faculties,
causing them all to attain realization and abide in samādhi.
Having performed this visualization, the practitioner forms the *utsargasamudra* mudrā at the crown of the head,
takes the rosary held in the hand and places it within the palms.
Placing the palms together at the heart, recite the mantra:
Oṃ vīrajñānamala svāhā. Recite this three times.
Having empowered the rosary, place it upon the crown of the head.
Thereafter, one should focus the mind:
with the left hand supporting the beads and the right hand moving them,
one should remain in accordance with every thought within the Samādhi of the Buddha-Mother.
Contemplate the mind without interruption.
Recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight or twenty-one times.
Once you have completed the count by using your prayer beads, [proceed].
Placing the rosary upon one’s head, set it down in its proper place,
and form the samādhi-mudrā by extending both hands horizontally with the right hand pressing over the left.
Place it below the navel;
straighten the body, close the eyes, and slightly incline the head forward.
Focus the mind upon the heart.
Contemplate clearly that upon the perfectly luminous mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna), which measures one cubit in length and breadth,
there gradually appear rows of inscribed characters pervading the entire dharma-realm;
contemplate them in sequence, turning to the right.
The radiance of each individual syllable shines through completely;
one contemplates from the outside toward the inside up to the syllable *dha*,
and then gradually from the inside toward the outside for all the syllables.
Cycling through this again and again,
by the third round the mind attains excellent tranquil concentration (*samādhi*),
clearly and distinctly contemplating the meaning of what is expressed.
Neither arising nor ceasing, each is equal and pervades the entire dharma realm.
Neither moving nor still, samādhi and prajñā are practiced in unison.
Forever free from all marks, this is the contemplation of the Prajñāpāramitā-samādhi.
From this point, form the seal of the Prajñāpāramitā of Desire;
recite the dhāraṇī seven times and scatter it over the crown of the head.
Next, form the seal of Universal Offering.
As before, perform the sequence of mental offerings;
then, in the presence of the noble assembly, dedicate all the merit produced through the aforementioned practices toward the fulfillment of all sought-after aspirations.
Having fulfilled the benefit of others for the sake of the state and the family,
one then dedicates [the merit] to sentient beings, to the adornment and purification of the Buddha-land,
to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and seeks supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
May all sentient beings together swiftly reach the other shore.
Next, bind the aforementioned boundary-sealing mudrā and recite the aforementioned mantra three times while turning to the left;
this immediately constitutes the dissolution of the boundary.
Next, bind the seals of the three preceding divisions and recite the aforementioned mantra three times, each time using the thumbs to push outward.
This constitutes the dismissal;
the holy assembly shall each return to their own original lands.
The practitioner should perform prostrations and depart.
As usual, they should practice walking meditation and uphold, receive, read, and recite the Mahāyāna,
without allowing the mind to become distracted or agitated.

All practices and vows shall be fully perfected. Chapter Five: The Visualization and Arrangement of the Syllables of the Dhāraṇī Wheel. If a practitioner is able, regarding this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, [to perform the following...]
A practitioner of yoga who cultivates wisdom should contemplate and examine every single phrase and every single syllable of this dhāraṇī from beginning to end.
Upon the pure, luminous, and perfectly clear Great Round Mirror within one's own mind,
visualize a golden wheel;
its outer first layer has sixteen spokes.
Visualize the sixteen phrases arranged in a clockwise sequence,
appearing with distinct clarity.
Next, the second layer has twelve spokes.
Visualize twelve syllables arranged in a clockwise rotation.
Next, arrange ten syllables in three successive tiers.
Within these ten syllables, there is the syllable *dhi*.
The intention here is that the preceding prose section,
up to the various assemblies of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and so forth,
is subsumed within sixteen phrases.
The sixteen phrases are subsumed into twelve characters;
the twelve characters are subsumed into ten characters;
and those ten characters are subsumed into a single character.
From the broad to the concise, it gradually diminishes and deepens until a single syllable manifests pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
for its nature and characteristics are equal, reaching the ultimate limit.
However, the practitioner contemplates the various Brahma-syllables,
making them clear and distinct, repeating them again and again.
If the mind is focused intently on the sequence of the curved strokes of these characters, [the signs will appear].
When the mind does not shift to other objects, the category of concentration (*samādhi*) is established;
when one contemplates the principles that are signified, the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) is established.
When these two factors are practiced in tandem, they manifest spontaneously, leading to unimpeded penetration and realization.
In every thought-moment, they eliminate all karmic obstructions, retributive obstructions, and afflictive obstructions;
their body and mind undergo transformation and reliance (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
attaining mastery and acquiring all supernatural powers until reaching the ultimate stage.
